attribution.note: Marcus's own sentence in his own post, endorsed.

semantics.note: This is an observation about what one study reported. Adding 'amid AI-assisted coding' matches the surrounding context about AI-written code. It does not turn the claim into a causal claim.

contract.note: Reading 'code quality' as maintainability indicators like churn and duplication is a fair, ordinary reading. The contract rightly separates observed changes from projections. The study isn't named, but GitClear fits the description closely.

evidence.note: The publisher's abstract (Jan 2024) reports worrying maintainability trends: more churn and less code reuse, in code written through Dec 2023.
The full report shows observed 2022-2023 rises in churn (+39%) and copy/paste, and less moved code. These are observed declines, not just 2024 projections. Causation isn't needed for this claim.

reviews.rationale: A study published before the post (GitClear, Jan 2024) reports observed worsening in code-quality indicators through 2023, alongside AI-assistant adoption. Marcus claimed only that one study indicates this, and that holds. The 2024 doubling is a projection, but the 2023 changes were observed.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The claim is rapid growth of harmful uses across the listed domains. 'Faster than I can report them' is rhetorical. 'Hallucinations may filter in' is hedged and not scored.

contract.note: No measure was named, so the plain reading applies: rapid overall expansion across several domains, not equal growth in each. That reading is fair and ordinary. The result depends on accepting discovery counts and expert reports as evidence of growth.

evidence.note: NewsGuard's tracked AI content-farm sites rose from under 50 (May 2023) to about 600 (Dec 2023) to 713 (Feb 2024), with ad revenue as the motive. These count discoveries, not new sites created.
WIRED (Jan 2024) documents AI imitation and summary books on Amazon. Industry experts describe them as increasing dramatically.
The NH attorney general's release documents AI voice-cloned robocalls telling people not to vote (Jan 2024). This shows election misuse exists, not how fast it is growing.
A March 2024 preprint shows a sharp rise in signs of LLM-assisted writing in papers, but does not measure harm or hallucinations.

reviews.rationale: In early 2024, dated counts show AI content-farm sites growing fast, and contemporary reporting shows AI fake books increasing. The election and science domains are also documented. Growth in the science domain is shown only as more AI-assisted writing, not proven harm. Taken together, harmful uses were spreading quickly across the named domains, as Marcus said.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The claim says software trading on creators' work is wrecking their careers, plus non-payment for training 'in many cases'. That makes it causal. Both qualifiers are kept.

contract.note: No measure was named. Reading 'careers wrecked' as severe damage to a livelihood is a fair, ordinary reading of firm language. It requires more than a minor drop in income.

evidence.note: This Aug 2023 summary of a freelancer study finds short-term drops in jobs and income (about 9% income loss). It shows harm but not wrecked careers, and does not link the harm to use of those freelancers' own work.
The Authors Guild's Oct 2023 filing alleges that most training used unlicensed works without pay. This is an advocacy group's allegation, not an independent record.
WaPo/Yahoo (Mar 2024) documents an influencer deepfake ad that was quickly removed. It does not measure any damage to her career.

reviews.rationale: The packet shows modest short-term income losses and an influencer impersonation, but no evidence that careers were severely wrecked by software exploiting those creators' work. Non-payment for training rests on an advocacy group's allegation. Nothing refutes the claim, so the evidence does not settle the causal claim either way.

attribution.note: Marcus's own words in his own post.

semantics.note: The factual core is that OpenAI asked the UK government for a copyright exemption. 'Brazenly' and 'all the gain' are evaluative and correctly left unscored.

contract.note: Distinguishing an argument that existing law already allows training from a request to change the law is fair. The result depends on whether Marcus meant the Dec 2023 House of Lords submission. He did not say which request he meant.

evidence.note: OpenAI's Dec 2023 House of Lords submission argues that current law permits training and says training is impossible without copyrighted material. Its copyright section asks for no exemption, but it cannot rule out other communications.
Guardian (Jan 2024) confirms the submission's argument under existing law. It reports no request for an exemption.
OpenAI's explicit call for a broad data-mining exception dates from 2025, after the post. It cannot count as evidence for the 2024 claim.

reviews.rationale: The one UK engagement identified in the window, the Dec 2023 Lords submission, argues that existing law permits training. It does not ask for an exemption, which points against Marcus's description. But the packet cannot confirm that this was the request he meant, and it cannot rule out other requests. The explicit exemption request came only in 2025. The case is not settled.
